title: Sell Mineral Rights in Longmont, CO
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Longmont, CO | DJ Basin Setback History
metaDescription: Own minerals near Longmont, CO? Its fracking fight shaped Colorado setback law. We evaluate that history and current well status before quoting your interest.
heroLead: Longmont has a unique place in Colorado oil and gas history: its 2012 voter-approved fracking ban was struck down by the state supreme court in 2016, and the fight over local control it triggered helped set the stage for the statewide overhaul that followed.
intro: If you hold minerals in or near Longmont, you own acreage in a place where the tension between local government authority and oil and gas development played out publicly and set legal precedent. The city's ban was overturned because state law then preempted local prohibitions, but that same conflict is part of why the legislature passed SB 19-181 in 2019, handing counties and cities real regulatory authority over siting, setbacks, and permitting that they didn't clearly have before.

sections.heading: What that history means for your interest today
paragraphs: Longmont and Boulder County now operate under stricter local oil and gas rules than much of Weld County, which affects where new wells can be sited relative to homes and schools. If your interest is tied to an existing, already-permitted well, that history mostly doesn't change its current production or value. If your acreage is undrilled, the local regulatory environment here is more restrictive than in Wattenberg's Weld County core, which affects development likelihood.
We check both angles: current COGCC well status tied to your legal description, and the applicable municipal or county setback rules if there's no existing well.

sections.heading: Production realities on existing Longmont-area wells
paragraphs: Where wells do exist near Longmont, they typically target the same Niobrara and Codell zones as the rest of the Wattenberg field, with the familiar steep early decline followed by a long stripper tail. We pull well-specific COGCC production data before quoting, since two wells drilled five years apart can be at very different points on that curve.

faqs.question: Does Longmont's old fracking ban still apply?
faqs.answer: No, it was overturned by the Colorado Supreme Court in 2016 on preemption grounds, though subsequent state law changes have given local governments other tools to regulate siting and setbacks.

faqs.question: Are Longmont-area setbacks stricter than Weld County's?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, reflecting Boulder County and city of Longmont policy choices under the local control authority granted by SB 19-181. That mainly affects new drilling potential, not existing wells.

faqs.question: Is my interest worth less because of the local regulatory environment?
faqs.answer: Only if it's undrilled acreage where new development is less likely. A currently producing interest is valued off its actual production regardless of local politics.
